cls: Synthetic non-steroidal estrogen prodrug - hormonal antineoplastic for prostate cancer
pharm: A water-soluble diphosphate prodrug of diethylstilbestrol that is dephosphorylated (notably by acid/prostatic phosphatase in prostatic tissue) to active diethylstilbestrol, which suppresses pituitary gonadotropin release and lowers testosterone, producing medical castration.
quick: Prostate cancer: oral ~120-240 mg/day; IV regimens of several hundred mg to ~1 g/day for short courses (per SmPC)
Take with or after food to reduce gastric upset
Contraindicated (used in men with prostate cancer)
Use with caution; limited specific data
Limit - additive hepatic and cardiovascular risk
Cardiovascular status, fluid retention, thromboembolism, LFTs, gynecomastia, PSA
summary: Fosfestrol (diethylstilbestrol diphosphate, fosfestrol tetrasodium) is a water-soluble phosphate prodrug of the synthetic non-steroidal estrogen diethylstilbestrol, used as hormonal therapy for advanced/metastatic prostate cancer. It is dephosphorylated to active diethylstilbestrol, with preferential activation by acid phosphatase in prostatic tissue, suppressing pituitary luteinizing hormone and reducing testosterone to castrate levels. It is given orally or by intravenous infusion (a high-dose IV course followed by oral maintenance is a classic regimen). Estrogen therapy carries significant risks of venous and arterial thromboembolism, fluid retention and cardiovascular events, gynecomastia and feminization, and hepatic effects, which have limited its first-line use in favor of LHRH analogues. It is NOT approved by the US FDA; dosing and safety information here are based on European/UK sources (SmPC/BNF) and historical literature.
indications: Palliative hormonal treatment of advanced or metastatic carcinoma of the prostate, particularly when other androgen-deprivation therapies are unsuitable or have failed

dosage.d: Approximately 120-240 mg daily (per product literature); maintenance dosing individualised
dosage.n: Doses vary by product; follow the specific SmPC

dosage.d: Several hundred milligrams up to about 1 g daily by slow IV infusion for a short course (e.g., 5 days), then switch to oral maintenance
dosage.t: Daily IV for a limited induction course
dosage.n: Give as a slow infusion; perineal pain during infusion is recognised

dosage.d: Lowest effective oral dose to maintain response
dosage.n: Titrate to response and tolerability; cardiovascular risk rises with dose

admin: Confirm the diagnosis and assess cardiovascular and thromboembolic risk before starting
Administer oral doses with or after food to reduce nausea and gastric irritation
Give intravenous doses by slow infusion as directed; transient perineal/anal pain during infusion is recognised and infusion rate may be slowed
Use the lowest effective dose to limit estrogenic cardiovascular and thromboembolic toxicity
Consider prophylactic breast irradiation before therapy to reduce gynecomastia where appropriate
Monitor for signs of fluid retention, heart failure, and thromboembolism throughout treatment
moa: Fosfestrol is the diphosphate ester prodrug of diethylstilbestrol (DES), a synthetic non-steroidal estrogen. The phosphate groups make it water-soluble and inactive until dephosphorylated by phosphatases; prostatic tissue is rich in acid phosphatase, giving some preferential local generation of active DES. DES acts as an estrogen-receptor agonist that suppresses hypothalamic-pituitary secretion of luteinizing hormone, reducing testicular testosterone production to castrate levels (medical castration). The resulting androgen deprivation slows growth of hormone-sensitive prostatic carcinoma. Estrogenic effects elsewhere account for fluid retention, gynecomastia, feminization, and prothrombotic/cardiovascular toxicity.

absolute: Active or prior venous or arterial thromboembolic disease (DVT, PE, MI, stroke)
Severe cardiovascular disease or uncontrolled heart failure
Severe hepatic impairment or active liver disease
Known estrogen-dependent malignancy other than the target prostate cancer (e.g., male breast cancer where contraindicated)
relative: Ischaemic heart disease, hypertension, or cardiac risk factors
Renal impairment or conditions aggravated by fluid retention
monitor: Cardiovascular status, blood pressure and signs of heart failure
Breast changes/gynecomastia; serum PSA and testosterone for treatment response

preg: Fosfestrol is used in men with prostate cancer; it is not indicated in women and is contraindicated in pregnancy. Diethylstilbestrol exposure in pregnancy is associated with serious adverse effects in offspring (including vaginal/cervical adenocarcinoma and genital tract abnormalities) and must be avoided.
lact: Not applicable to the indicated male population; estrogens are contraindicated during breastfeeding because they are excreted in milk and suppress lactation.
renal: There is limited specific information; use with caution in renal impairment, particularly because estrogen-induced fluid retention may worsen renal or cardiac conditions. No well-defined dose adjustment is established.
hepatic: Estrogens are metabolized hepatically and can cause cholestasis and worsen liver function. Fosfestrol should be avoided in severe hepatic impairment or active liver disease and used with caution where liver function is compromised; monitor liver function tests.

major: Anticoagulants - estrogens alter coagulation factors and may oppose anticoagulant effect; combined thromboembolic and bleeding risk requires careful monitoring
Other prothrombotic or cardiovascular-risk drugs - additive thromboembolic/cardiovascular risk
moderate: Hepatic enzyme inducers (rifampicin, carbamazepine, phenytoin, St John's wort) - may reduce estrogen levels
CYP3A4 inhibitors - may increase estrogen exposure
Antihypertensives - estrogen-induced fluid retention may reduce their effect
minor: May alter requirements for antidiabetic agents
interactions.food: Take with or after food to reduce gastrointestinal upset.
interactions.alcohol: Limit alcohol - additive hepatic and cardiovascular risk.
interactions.diagnostics: Estrogens alter coagulation, thyroid-binding globulin, and other endocrine/lipid laboratory tests; suppresses serum testosterone and reduces PSA in responders.

common: Loss of libido and erectile dysfunction
serious: Congestive heart failure from fluid retention
rare: Worsening of pre-existing epilepsy or migraine
emergency: Acute pulmonary embolism or deep vein thrombosis

monitoring: Cardiovascular assessment, blood pressure and signs of heart failure throughout treatment
Vigilance for venous and arterial thromboembolism
Body weight and peripheral edema (fluid retention)
Serum PSA and testosterone for treatment response; calcium in bony metastatic disease
counsel: This hormone treatment shrinks prostate cancer by lowering male hormone levels
Report promptly any leg swelling or pain, chest pain, sudden breathlessness, or weakness/slurred speech - these could be a clot
Breast swelling or tenderness, reduced sex drive and fluid retention are expected effects of this hormone
Tell your doctor if you gain weight rapidly, become breathless, or have ankle swelling
Take oral doses with food, and keep your clinic and blood-test appointments
Tell your doctor about all other medicines, especially blood thinners
pk: Testosterone suppression develops over days to a few weeks
Active diethylstilbestrol generated after dephosphorylation of the prodrug
Estrogenic suppression of gonadotropins persists during continued dosing
Store as directed by the product; protect from light and moisture
pearls: NOT FDA-approved - dosing/safety here are from European/UK sources (SmPC/BNF) and historical literature; verify against the local product label
Fosfestrol is a phosphate prodrug of diethylstilbestrol; prostatic acid phosphatase gives some local activation
Dominant risk is thromboembolic and cardiovascular - assess and counsel on clot warning signs; largely superseded by LHRH analogues
Gynecomastia is common; prophylactic breast irradiation before therapy can reduce it
Transient perineal/anal pain can occur during intravenous infusion - slow the infusion rate
Use the lowest effective dose to limit estrogenic cardiovascular toxicity
missed: If you miss an oral dose, take it as soon as you remember unless it is almost time for the next dose, in which case skip the missed dose. Do not double up. Tell your hospital team if you miss doses, as this affects hormone control of the cancer.
overdose: Overdose would intensify estrogenic effects - severe nausea, fluid retention, and increased thromboembolic and cardiovascular risk. There is no specific antidote; management is supportive with discontinuation of the drug, monitoring for and treatment of thromboembolism and fluid overload, and supportive cardiovascular and hepatic care.
